subject: Climate & Environment
title: Plastic in the Water
description: A fast breakdown of Plastic in the Water for builders.

hook.text: Every year, 11 million tons of plastic enter the ocean. That is a garbage truck per minute.

buildup.text: Plastic doesn't decompose — it breaks into smaller and smaller pieces called microplastics.

discovery.text: Microplastics have been found in fish, shellfish, drinking water, and human blood.

twist.text: Only 9% of all plastic ever made has been recycled. The rest is in landfills, burned, or loose.

climax.text: By 2050, the ocean could contain more plastic by weight than fish.

punchline.text: Plastic never goes away. It just gets smaller and harder to find.

quiz.question: How much plastic enters the ocean each year?

details.summary: Over 10 million tonnes of plastic enter oceans annually, and microplastics now contaminate rivers, lakes, tap water, and bottled water worldwide. Plastic pollution harms marine life, enters the food chain, and carries toxic chemicals that leach into water sources over time.
details.whyItMatters: Plastic pollution in water is ubiquitous and growing. Microplastics have been found in human blood and organs, raising concerns about long-term health impacts that science is only beginning to understand.
takeaways: Over 10 million tonnes of plastic enter oceans each year
Microplastics are found in tap water and bottled water
Plastic carries toxic chemicals that leach into water

faq.question: How do microplastics get into drinking water?
faq.answer: Plastic breaks down into tiny fragments through UV exposure and physical weathering. These particles enter watersheds through runoff, wastewater, and atmospheric deposition. Conventional water treatment removes some but not all microplastics from drinking supplies.

faq.question: Are microplastics in water harmful to health?
faq.answer: Research is ongoing, but studies have found microplastics in human blood, lungs, and placentas. They may carry toxic additives and pollutants. The WHO says current levels in drinking water pose low risk, but long-term exposure effects are not yet fully understood.
